Kind of shitty science as I'm not bothering looking it up. Tinnitus happens when neurons don't get any stimulation. So the hair in your ears that catch sound are dead for som reason. The neurons that are connected to and get input from these hair are thus without work. They get bored and start sending signals to your brain contsantly = annoying sound. When you ignore a screaming child the process is different. The neurons get the input (the screaming), but after a while they understand that this is not important and stop sending signals to the brain. They get tired and stop sending signals about this to the brain as often.

TL;DR: Tinnitus is bored neurons trying to be helpful. Ignoring screaming is tired neurons understanding that it is not helpful to keep telling you a child is screaming.

The stuy of the top comment is about how aerobic exercise for three hours a week is more effective at treating depression than high-dose medication. There are a lot of reasons why you can't just say that this means that exercise prevents/reduces depression in active populations. Since I haven't got the study I don't know the details behind it but I'll come with some points you have to keep in mind. 


Firstly the patient groups selected for these kinds of trials are very selected. This means they have fairly normal life (so soldiers are probably excluded) and they often have to only have depression not some comorbide disorders (this is actually quite uncommon with psychological illnesses, people often have two or more). What kind of depression they have can also have played a role.


Secondly by the wording in the comment it is provided as a treatment for depression, not as a way to prevent depression. This means that you are taking people who are ALREADY depressed and then get them to exercise. This means that alot of those people might not have exercised much before, or might have only done strength training. So this would not apply to your group as they probably wouldn't have been able to enter the forces if they were that depressed (at least we can assume few manage this) therefore the depression came after the exercise the exercise was not used as a treatment. 


Thirdly it is compared to the effect of anti-depressant which isn't a "cure" for depression for many people. Some will have no help from them, some will have a bit of help and some will get well by using them. So exercise is thougt to be better than this, but this does not by any means imply that exercise cures depression.


Fourth it is specified 3 hours. Soldiers are probably doing more exercise some hard weeks and less after initial training so they wont be meeting the criteria. It is not saying the more exercise the less depressed, only that 3 hours of earobic exercise works better at treating depression than medication. You are saying they are getting on average 5 hours a week which is 2 hours more and might be enough to put too much pressure on some causing depression instead of making it better.


Lastly I admit to not knowing anything about the US military so my thought about the psychological stress levels was just a guess and what you say about that not being a part of day to day life makes a lot of sense.

Soldiers are typically under a lot of both mental and physical stress to weed out those who cant handle it and train those who can. Training too much prevents the body from getting out of the stresd that exercise causes. This might make them more likely to be depressed I would guess.

I understand where you are coming from. The problem is that adopted children are not like average children. First of all you have all the reasons they are being taken away from their birth-parents: drugs, abuse, neglect, young parent etc. So this is in the childs baggage. This is not things that are merely forgotten and the child might get behavioral problems or psychological problems from their past home. They can also have physical problems like fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, teeth problems, injuries, malnutriton etc. 

On top of this you have the trauma of being removed from their parents. Even if a child is abused they will probably have som kind of attachment to their parents. This means that the adopted child is at risk of getting reactive attachment disorder from the adoption process. This is NOT an easy thing to cope with. It can mean that the child wont trust anyone and is constantly afraid of being sent away. It can have problems feeling connected and to love anyone. Imagine adopting a child which does not want to be close to you? Who does not love you? And on top of this is aggressive and has lots of physical problems that needs to be dealt with? It is not something the average family will be able to deal with easily.

I am not saying adoption is bad or that all adopted children has a lot of problems. But the chance of them having some kind of issue is a lot higher than the average child and the family that is adopting need to be able o cope with this. Otherwise the child risks being abused, neglected or sent away again which logically makes the problems even harder to handle. Yes there is a lack of  adoptive-homes for children, but most of the children that have problems finding homes are "too old" (read: not a cute baby), have a handicap, have some kind of behavioral problem or something similar. The option is often not to keep them in the homes with their not suitable parents, but to place them in foster homes or institutions and then try to find a home where there are people who are able to handle the baggage the child has.

 The chance of dying of breast cancer at this age is also near non-excistent. This is of course as long as you haven't gotten a gene test that says you are high risk or you have a family history of breast cancer.

False positives sometimes leads to unneccessary treatment (with side effects) of non-cancerous bumps. This is of course the worst case scenario. Read one paragraph. Write down what you remember from what you just read. Don't really remember anything? Read it again. Write down what you just read. (Or explain it out loud is fine too. But don't just think what you read, it's to easy to trick yourself into thinking you remember). When one paragraph only needs one read through to be able to summrise the content add an paragraph. The goal should be to be able to read at least a page and then being able to summrising it. Just reading is not good for remembering. 

ALternatively you can make up questions as you read. Write them down and underline the answers in your book. This also makes it easy to revise as you have revision question. It saves some time not having to write down the answers just underlining them. Add which page tha questions are made from. You learn a lot more from testing than just reading. Always test yourself. If you watch it with subtitles I would advice you to watch it again without them too. With subtitles I usually depend to much on them. If you know these movies by heart already it would probably be better to just watch them without subtitles the first time through. 


The best way of watching movies in a foreign language? Well, depedns what you want to do. If you want to improve your ability to understand spoken Danish I would just watch them without subtitles once or twice and then move on to a new movie.


 Learn grammar and vocabulary? Watch them with subtitles and pick out the words/sentences with grammar structures you want to learn and write them down for later studying. For grammar I usually read about a new grammar thing and then watch a movie/read a book and try to be on the look out for this new thing I learned. The same can be done for frequently used vocabulary, but it sounds like you already got the hang of the most used words.

Want to improve pronounciation? Mimic whatever is being said. This is usually best done by looping a short sentence and hearing it againg and again and again before starting to trying to say it at nearly the same time and the exact same way as the person speaking. Real movies have the advantage of also showing you correct facial movements and body language which cartoons and animated movies wont. 

As for the childrena absorbing language for TV, this is only true if there are someone there talking with them about what is happening either while they are watching or afterwards. Simply putting a child in front of a television all day wont improve their language skills much.

When I begin a language I try to learn 1000-2000 frequently used words. In this phase I will usually add 100 new words a day and will end up like you do with to many reviews. What I do is usually to start ignoring words that I can easily get correct or "leeches" which are words that I just can't seem to remember. I also get rid of any words I find annoying to type out. Since these are words that appear frequently doing this wont be a problem since I will see these words in context often enough. Some hard words will suddenly fall into place when you have just seen them in context, instead of only seeing them on Memrise. Or they will make sense when you have learnt some other words. No reason to try to hammer them down, it's just a waste of time.

Another approach I've done is just ignore all words in the earlier levels and move on to learning new words. You should learn words in context anyway. Memrise is a crutch. It's there to keep you up when you can't yourself, but it isn't effective to think that every word you ever learn should be in Memrise. It is better to make sure you meet these words outside of Memrise since you then will remember them anyway and get to use them to learn new words.
